title: Macromolecule structure
examples: What is the difference between a peptide bond and an ester bond?
How many levels of structure are there for a protein?
Can you explain how the bonds hold the final shape of a protein?

explain.say: Today we are looking at how large biological molecules are built.
First we will look at the peptide bond linking amino acids together.
Next we examine the glycosidic bond found in carbohydrates like starch.
Then we study the ester bond connecting fatty acids to glycerol in fats.
Proteins have four levels of structure that determine their function.
For example, the primary structure is just the linear chain of amino acids.

faq.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary protein structure?
faq.a: The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids. The secondary structure describes local folding patterns like alpha-helices.
asks: Can you show me the difference between the two?

faq.q: Are all bonds in macromolecules the same type?
faq.a: No, different bonds link different types of molecules. For instance, peptide bonds link amino acids together.
asks: Is the bond in DNA the same as in proteins?

faq.q: Why is the tertiary structure so important for a protein?
faq.a: The tertiary structure gives the protein its unique, functional three-dimensional shape. This shape is necessary for it to work correctly.
asks: Does the 3D shape change if it gets hot?
What happens if the shape is wrong?

faq.q: How many types of bonds do we need to know?
faq.a: We need to know the peptide, glycosidic, and ester bonds. Each one links different biological molecules together.
asks: Are there more than three types?

faq.q: Does the quaternary structure always exist?
faq.a: No, not all proteins have a quaternary structure. It only exists if the protein is made of multiple separate subunits.
asks: What are subunits in this context?

facts: The peptide bond links amino acids to form a polypeptide chain.
The glycosidic bond connects monosaccharides to form larger carbohydrates.
The ester bond links fatty acids to glycerol in lipids.
Protein structure has four levels: primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary.

quiz.say: A molecule made of many sugar units linked by a bond is called:
quiz.why: This bond specifically links sugar units together in carbohydrates.

wrong.0: While present, this is a weaker interaction, not the primary covalent linkage.
wrong.2: This bond is used to link amino acids, not sugars.
wrong.3: This bond is found in fats and oils.

quiz.say: If a protein has four separate parts working together, which structure level is it?
quiz.why: This level describes the arrangement of multiple polypeptide chains.

wrong.1: The tertiary structure is the folding of a single chain into 3D space.
wrong.2: The secondary structure refers to local folding like helices or sheets.
wrong.3: This only describes the simple, linear order of amino acids.

quiz.say: The bond formed between a carboxyl group and an amino group is the:
quiz.why: This specific reaction forms the backbone of all proteins.

wrong.0: This bond is formed between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.
wrong.1: While charged groups interact, the covalent linkage is the peptide bond.
wrong.3: This bond is formed between sugar molecules.
